unit1: Commercial operation: 2 September 1974. Permanent shutdown: 20 September 2019.
unit2: Commercial operation: 30 December 1978. Permanent shutdown: 28 March 1979.
costs: A Corporate History of Three Mile Island
TMI-1 entered service in September 1974 for $400 million. TMI-2 construction cost $700 million.
accident: 5 Facts to Know About Three Mile Island
Equipment failure and operator error caused a partial meltdown at Unit 2 on March 28, 1979; regulatory training and emergency-planning changes followed.
smithsonian: Three Mile Island: The Inside Story — Five Score Years of Nuclear Power
Unit 1 was permitted to return to service in October 1985. Unit 2 was placed in post-defueling monitored storage in 1993.
cleanup: Unit 1 restarted in October 1985. Unit 2 cleanup ended in December 1993 before monitored storage; this did not restore the damaged unit to operation.
dep: Unit 1 shut down September 20, 2019. The planned restart applies to Unit 1 and requires regulatory reviews.
announcement: Constellation to Launch Crane Clean Energy Center, Restoring Jobs and Carbon-Free Power to The Grid
September 20, 2024: Constellation announced a 20-year Microsoft power agreement enabling the proposed 835 MW Unit 1 restart. The original target was 2028.
capex: The company estimated approximately $1.6 billion in capital expenditures to restart Crane.
progress: August 6, 2026: Constellation reported FERC approval for transferring capacity interconnection rights and an NRC fuel license amendment; it still targeted 2027 operations.
operator: The operator expects readiness for service in 2027, subject to approvals. Unit 1 is independent of accident-damaged Unit 2. The official photo library includes operator training photographs.
loan: Energy Department Closes Loan to Restart Nuclear Power Plant in Pennsylvania
November 18, 2025: DOE closed a $1 billion loan to help finance the 835 MW Crane restart, subject to licensing approvals.

events.title: Three Mile Island Unit 1 Begins Commercial Operation
events.description: Unit 1 begins commercial operation on Three Mile Island in Pennsylvania, following construction that began in 1968.
events.body:
This is Unit 1, the reactor later renamed Crane Clean Energy Center. The reactor database distinguishes its June 1974 grid connection from its September 2 commercial start.

Historical construction cost: USD 400 million. Three Mile Island Alert reports “at a cost of $400 million”; this is the original unit cost in stated dollars, without inflation or currency conversion.

refs.title: A Corporate History of Three Mile Island
refs.reasoning: Historical Unit 1 construction cost quote: “at a cost of  $400 million”.

events.title: Three Mile Island Unit 2 Begins Commercial Operation
events.description: Three Mile Island’s second reactor enters commercial service, less than three months before its 1979 accident.
events.body:
The reactor database dates first grid connection to April 21, 1978 and commercial operation to December 30, 1978.

Historical construction cost: USD 700 million. Three Mile Island Alert states “TMI-2 was built at a cost to rate payers of $700 million”. This is construction cost, excluding subsequent cleanup.

refs.title: A Corporate History of Three Mile Island
refs.reasoning: Unit 2 construction cost quote: “TMI-2 was built at a cost to rate payers of $700 million”.

events.title: Three Mile Island Unit 2 Suffers a Partial Meltdown
events.description: Equipment failures and operator errors cause inadequate core cooling and a partial meltdown in Unit 2, permanently ending that reactor’s operation.
events.body:
A relief valve remained open while instrumentation misled operators about its state. Loss of coolant and inadequate circulation damaged the core. DOE describes subsequent changes to operator training, emergency planning and equipment requirements.

The accident damaged Unit 2. The later Crane restart project concerns the separate Unit 1 reactor.

refs.title: 5 Facts to Know About Three Mile Island
Crane Clean Energy Center
refs.reasoning: Distinguishes the independent Unit 1 restart from damaged Unit 2.

events.title: Three Mile Island Unit 1 Returns to Service After Six-Year Shutdown
events.description: The undamaged Unit 1 returns to service in October 1985 after extended regulatory proceedings, modifications and retraining.
events.body:
The Smithsonian chronology places permission to return to service in October 1985; the World Nuclear Association also dates the restart to that month. Unit 1 had been shut for refueling when Unit 2’s accident occurred.

October 1 is a month-only timeline anchor, not a verified restart day. No separate published budget for this return-to-service event was established.

refs.title: Three Mile Island: The Inside Story — Five Score Years of Nuclear Power
refs.reasoning: Chronology states October 1985; the exact day is not supplied.

events.title: Three Mile Island Unit 2 Enters Post-Defueling Monitored Storage
events.description: Unit 2 moves into monitored storage in December 1993 after the initial accident cleanup; decommissioning remains a separate, later process.
events.body:
The cleanup removed damaged fuel and processed contaminated water. World Nuclear Association dates the transition to post-defueling monitored storage to December 1993. Monitored storage did not mean the site was fully decommissioned or Unit 2 restored to operation.

December 1 represents month-level evidence; an exact transition day is not established. No construction price is assigned to this storage milestone.

refs.title: Three Mile Island Accident
refs.reasoning: Dates post-defueling monitored storage to December 1993; exact day unspecified.

events.title: Three Mile Island Unit 1 Shuts Down for Economic Reasons
events.description: Unit 1 shuts down on September 20, 2019, ending electricity generation at Three Mile Island until any future approved restart.
events.body:
Pennsylvania DEP records September 20, 2019 as the Unit 1 shutdown date. Constellation’s later restart announcement says the retirement was economic.

This closure was separate from the 1979 accident that permanently disabled Unit 2. The closure event has no construction price.

refs.title: Constellation to Launch Crane Clean Energy Center, Restoring Jobs and Carbon-Free Power to The Grid
refs.reasoning: Says Unit 1 shut for economic reasons exactly five years before September 20, 2024.

events.title: Microsoft Deal Launches Three Mile Island Unit 1 Restart Plan
events.description: Constellation announces a 20-year Microsoft power agreement and plans to restart Unit 1 as Crane Clean Energy Center, restoring about 835 MW.
events.body:
The September 20 announcement originally targeted 2028. This pin dates the agreement and restart plan; it does not claim electricity generation resumed that day.

Restart capital estimate: USD 1.6 billion. Constellation’s results state “approximately $1.6 billion of cash from operations for capital expenditures necessary to restart the plant”. The separate USD 1 billion DOE loan is financing, not the total project cost.

refs.title: Constellation to Launch Crane Clean Energy Center, Restoring Jobs and Carbon-Free Power to The Grid
Constellation Reports Third Quarter 2024 Results
refs.reasoning: Restart capex quote: “approximately $1.6 billion of cash from operations for capital expenditures necessary to restart the plant”.

events.title: Constellation Reports Crane Restart Interconnection and Fuel-License Milestones
events.description: Constellation reports FERC approval for an interconnection-rights transfer and NRC approval of a fuel-license amendment while maintaining its 2027 restart target.
events.body:
The August 6 results report these regulatory milestones. The date here is the dated company report, not an inferred date for either individual approval. These steps do not constitute final permission to restart.

The overall Unit 1 restoration budget is USD 1.6 billion, rather than a new budget for these approvals: “approximately $1.6 billion of cash from operations for capital expenditures necessary to restart the plant”.

refs.title: Constellation Reports Third Quarter 2024 Results
refs.reasoning: Overall restart budget, not incremental approval spending: “approximately $1.6 billion of cash from operations for capital expenditures necessary to restart the plant”.
